title: MicroVerse: Video Models for Microscale Biology
one_liner: Building a video model that respects the laws of biology by training it on a carefully curated dataset of microscale phenomena.
lead: Video models can generate smooth, coherent videos of everyday scenes. But when you ask them to simulate what happens inside a cell or inside an organ, they fail badly—making things that violate the laws of physics or biology. This paper shows why that happens and builds a specialized video model that can accurately simulate microscale biology.

problem.h2: Video models trained on humans fail on cells
paras: Modern video generation models are trained almost entirely on human-scale videos: people walking, driving, playing sports. They learn patterns like how light behaves, how clothes move, how faces change expression. But cells and organs follow completely different rules—they are often transparent, move with diffusion and flow rather than rigid motion, and obey different timescales.

A naive approach is to take a pre-trained video model and just ask it to generate microscale scenes. It fails. The output violates laws of physics (objects appear and vanish, momentum goes wrong, diffusion spreads backwards). It is temporally inconsistent (the same cell looks different frame to frame). And it simply does not match what microscale phenomena actually look like.

callout.html: Models trained on everyday videos lack the biological knowledge to simulate what is actually inside a cell.

steps.text: Download 8,000 YouTube videos tagged with microscale biology (organ, cell, molecule).
Use an LLM to generate 459 criteria (does it obey physics? match biology?). Experts vote and refine.
Automatic filters remove corrupted clips; experts remove unphysical ones. 9,601 verified videos remain.
A multimodal LLM describes each video in detail (150 words); experts verify each description.
Train a video diffusion model on this biology-grounded dataset with the rubric guiding the training objective.

paras: The paper changes one thing: the training data and the training objective. Instead of training a video model on generic internet video, the authors train it on 9,601 expert-verified videos of actual microscale phenomena, paired with biology-aware captions and constrained by physics-respecting evaluation criteria.

hidden.name: how much a generated video violates the laws of physics
paras: The paper introduces a hidden quantity: how often does a generated video break the laws of physics and biology? This is not just a single number; it is a multi-dimensional measurement. The benchmark includes 459 expert-annotated criteria grouped into dimensions: scientific fidelity (does the biology stay correct?), visual quality (is it clear and artifact-free?), and instruction-following (does it match the description?).

The paper estimates this quantity by having experts score each generated video on the rubric. A general-purpose video model scores poorly (high violations). MicroVerse scores much higher because it was trained on videos that already respect these physical laws.

heat.caption: Darker means the criterion is violated more often. MicroVerse is darker on fidelity and physics.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the score a video gets when experts check it against 459 biology-aware criteria. Ordinary video models score low; MicroVerse scores high.
The benchmark adds up all the criterion scores, giving more weight to the most important ones (chosen by experts). Violations of physical law contribute large negative penalties to the total.

mechanism.h2: Why training on the right data works
paras: The mechanism is simple: models learn from what they see. A video model trained on everyday human-scale videos learns patterns like rigid objects, lighting from above, familiar physics. When asked to generate a cell, it falls back on those learned patterns—and they are wrong for biology.

By training a video model on 9,601 real videos of cells and organs, the model learns the actual patterns of microscale biology: how diffusion spreads (not rigid motion), how transparency changes (not like solid objects), how timescales work (millions of atoms move together). The expert-verified captions teach the model which description matches which biology. The rubric-guided training objective rewards the model for generating videos that satisfy the 459 physics and biology criteria.
This works because machine learning models are data-driven: the patterns in the training data become the patterns the model generates. Biology-grounded data produces biology-grounded output.

stages.s: Text prompt: describe a cell mitosis
Model encodes prompt into a dense representation
Denoising model removes noise step by step from compressed video
Decoder converts compressed representation back to pixel video
Output: video of mitosis that respects biology

math.words: minimize the difference between the model's noise prediction and the actual noise injected into videos, weighted by how well the output satisfies biology criteria
symbols: the compressed video representation (made smaller to save memory) with noise added, at step t
the random noise that was added to corrupt the video
the model's guess of what noise was there
which denoising step (0 means pure noise, T means the original clear video)
the compact encoding of the text description

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a video frame of a mitosing cell is encoded into 256 numbers (a compressed representation).
At step 50 of the denoising process (halfway through), random noise is added, corrupting the representation.
The model tries to predict what noise was added: it guesses 256 noise values.
The true noise was different; the error is large.
The model's weights are nudged to predict more accurately next time.
After many iterations on many videos, the model learns that 'mitosis' in the text description should predict a certain pattern of noise at each step.
When answering a new question, the model is given pure noise and a text prompt, then predicts and removes noise 50 times to reconstruct a biology-consistent video.

math.note: The equation is standard diffusion training. The difference is training it on biology-verified data with a rubric-guided objective.

items.html: If the text description does not specify a clear biological mechanism, the model generates plausible-looking but incorrect dynamics. The rubric catches this because the output will not match domain expertise.

items.b: Dataset too small for uncommon phenomena.
items.html: The dataset has 9,601 videos across three scales (organ, cell, molecule). Very uncommon or specialized biological scenarios may not appear in training because they are so rare, so the model has never encountered the patterns needed to generate them and produces unreliable or incorrect results.

If the training videos are biased toward certain organisms or cell types, the model has seen those much more often and will be accurate on them, but will fail on organisms or cells it rarely or never encountered. The paper does not report which organisms appear most in the dataset.

Pair any video generation model with a curated, expert-verified, physics-grounded dataset and a rubric-based training objective. The model will learn to generate videos that respect the laws of the domain it sees.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a microscale simulation demo: download a video generation model (Wan2.1), fine-tune it on the MicroSim-10K dataset (or a subset), and generate videos of a cell undergoing mitosis or a protein folding. Compare its output to ground-truth videos on the rubric dimensions: does the output obey conservation of mass? Do organelles stay visible and move smoothly? Does the description match the generated dynamics?
demo.closing: The demo makes it impossible to miss: a model trained on everyday video generates cells that flicker and vanish because it never learned the right patterns; the same model fine-tuned on biology-grounded data generates cells that behave like actual cells because it has now seen how real biology works.
